modelAnswer: A chemical reaction occurs through molecular collisions between reactant particles. For a reaction to proceed, colliding molecules must possess sufficient energy equal to or greater than the activation energy ($E_a$), which is the minimum energy barrier that must be overcome. When molecules collide with adequate energy, they form an activated complex (transition state), an unstable, high-energy intermediate configuration where old bonds are partially broken and new bonds are partially formed. The enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) of the reaction depends on the energy balance: bond breaking is endothermic (requires energy) while bond formation is exothermic (releases energy). If energy released from forming new bonds exceeds energy consumed in breaking old bonds, the reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$) and releases heat to surroundings. Conversely, if more energy is required to break bonds than is released forming new ones, the reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$) and absorbs heat. Only collisions with energy $\geq E_a$ successfully form the activated complex and proceed to products, determining the reaction rate and overall energy transfer between system and surroundings.

modelAnswer: **Collision Theory** explains how chemical reactions occur through molecular collisions. For a reaction to proceed, reactant molecules must collide with sufficient energy (exceeding the **activation energy**, $E_a$) and proper orientation. During collision, reactants form an **activated complex** (transition state), an unstable, high-energy intermediate where old bonds are partially broken and new bonds are partially formed. The activation energy is the minimum energy required to reach this activated complex state. After the activated complex forms, it either decomposes to products (releasing energy) or reverts to reactants. The **heat of reaction** ($\Delta H$) is the net energy difference between products and reactants: if products are lower in energy than reactants, the reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$); if products are higher in energy, the reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$). The activation energy is independent of $\Delta H$, a reaction with high $E_a$ may still be exothermic, and vice versa. Catalysts lower the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway, increasing reaction rate without affecting the heat of reaction.

modelAnswer:
**First Law of Thermodynamics:** The first law of thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another. For a system, the change in internal energy equals the heat absorbed by the system minus the work done by the system.

**Mathematical Expression:**
$$\Delta U = q - w$$

Alternatively: $\Delta U = q + w$ (when work is done on the system)

Where: $\Delta U$ = change in internal energy, $q$ = heat absorbed by system, $w$ = work done by system

**Application to Gas in Cylinder with Moveable Piston:**

Consider a gas confined in a cylinder with a moveable piston. When the gas is heated, it absorbs heat energy ($q$). This energy is used in two ways: (1) to increase the internal energy of the gas molecules ($\Delta U$), and (2) to do work against external pressure by pushing the piston outward ($w$).

The internal energy change depends on temperature change of the gas. The work done by the gas expands the volume against atmospheric pressure. Therefore: $\Delta U = q - w$

**Derivation of $W = P\Delta V$:**

When the piston moves outward by distance $dx$, the work done by gas is:
$$dw = F \cdot dx = P \cdot A \cdot dx$$

Since $A \cdot dx = dV$ (change in volume):
$$dw = P \cdot dV$$

For finite volume change at constant pressure:
$$W = P(V_f - V_i) = P\Delta V$$

This represents the work done by the gas during expansion against constant external pressure.

Consider a gas confined in a cylinder with a moveable piston. When the gas is heated, it absorbs heat energy ($q$). This energy is used in two ways: (1) to increase the internal energy of the gas molecules ($\Delta U$), and (2) to do work against external pressure by pushing the piston outward ($w$).

The internal energy change depends on temperature change of the gas. The work done by the gas expands the volume against atmospheric pressure. Therefore: $\Delta U = q - w$

**Derivation of $W = P\Delta V$:**

When the piston moves outward by distance $dx$, the work done by gas is:
$$dw = F \cdot dx = P \cdot A \cdot dx$$

Since $A \cdot dx = dV$ (change in volume):
$$dw = P \cdot dV$$

For finite volume change at constant pressure:
$$W = P(V_f - V_i) = P\Delta V$$

This represents the work done by the gas during expansion against constant external pressure.

$NaCl_{(s)} \longrightarrow Na^+_{(aq)} + Cl^-_{(aq)}$
$S^{\circ}(NaCl) = 72.1\text{ J/mol/K}, S^{\circ}(Na^+) = 321\text{ J/mol/K}, S^{\circ}(Cl^-) = 56.5\text{ J/mol/K}$

keyPoints: ["(a) CO2(g) -> CO2(s): ΔS is negative (gas to solid decreases disorder).","(b) 2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l): ΔS is negative (3 mol gas -> 2 mol liquid, large decrease in disorder and moles of gas).","(c) H2O(l) -> H2O(g): ΔS is positive (liquid to gas increases disorder)."]
stem: For which of the following reactions is delta-S standard positive or negative? (a) CO2(g) -> CO2(s), (b) 2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l), (c) H2O(l) -> H2O(g).

keyPoints: ["Increasing entropy order: CH3OH(s) < CH3OH(l) < CH3OH(g).","Entropy increases from solid to liquid to gas because molecular disorder and freedom of motion increase at each stage."]
stem: Arrange CH3OH(s), CH3OH(g), and CH3OH(l) in order of increasing entropy. Justify your order.

keyPoints: ["Using ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, a reaction is spontaneous when ΔG is negative.","If ΔH is negative and ΔS is positive, the reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures. If ΔH is positive and ΔS is negative, it is never spontaneous. Mixed-sign cases depend on temperature (e.g. exothermic with decreasing entropy is spontaneous only at low T)."]
stem: Develop a hypothetical reaction and calculate the Gibbs free energy. Discuss the conditions under which the reaction would be spontaneous or non-spontaneous.

keyPoints: ["Enthalpy (H) tracks heat content at constant pressure; entropy (S) tracks disorder/randomness; Gibbs free energy (G = H - TS) combines both to predict reaction spontaneity.","A good review should connect these three quantities through ΔG = ΔH - TΔS and explain how each is measured or calculated (calorimetry for ΔH, statistical/thermodynamic tables for ΔS)."]
stem: Research and review the fundamental concepts of enthalpy, entropy, and Gibbs free energy.
